utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Groome: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 1505, when we interrupted your testimony last week, you were beginning to describe a column of Muslim civilians from the Visegrad municipality that made their way into Visegrad town. Could I ask you to resume at that point and please describe what you know about that column of people that walked into Visegrad town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just if I might interrupt the witness. I see that the voice distortion has been set up. As you'll recall, the witness agreed that it was no longer necessary and we could proceed without voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the registry could deal with that, please. While we're dealing with that, Mr. Nice, we omitted yesterday to regulate Exhibit 526.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I had that in mind afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So at a convenient time this morning or relatively soon, we ought to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or even this afternoon, maybe. But I think the position is this: That all exhibits bar numbers 27 and 28 are referred to in the witness's report. I'll check that. 27 and 28 were covered by him in evidence without being specifically referred to as exhibits in order that I could save time, but they were dealt with, they being the orders for sitting in Belgrade rather than elsewhere, and I'd ask that they be admitted as well on the basis that they've been effectively covered. But I will check or have checked that literally every other of the exhibits is covered in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Subject to your checking -- just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you would check, Mr. Nice, to ensure that there are -- there is nothing which wasn't referred to. Subject to that checking and your reporting to us, all the exhibits will be admitted as the binder stands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could I please ask you to address that question now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. So when Captain Vuksavljevic, who was commander of the dam, received orders from Colonel Ojdanic to the effect that he could move towards Brstanica and get this column of civilians out, if I can put it that way, he indeed did set out with two military trucks, and there were about 30 soldiers there. We came to Brstanica. A column was formed there. We were all in a hurry so everything went very fast. Most people went on foot and some took cars and everybody set out for town. As we were approaching town, a lot of gunfire was heard in the area that we were supposed to go through as we were moving towards town. At that moment Captain Vuksavljevic said we should go on further and that he would go in the direction from where the gunfire was coming from and that he would see what this was all about and he would resolve the problems that we might possibly have during our journey, and that's exactly the way it was. In this organised column led by these soldiers, people went to the town football stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before I ask you about the football stadium, can you approximate the number of people that were in this column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this column, there were approximately 400 persons. How can I put this? It was mostly the local population from that area; women, children, elderly people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the column cross the old Turkish bridge crossing the Drina into Visegrad town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They had to cross that bridge along that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard evidence from a Serb journalist regarding his observations regarding a column. My question to you is: Are you aware of any other column that crossed the old Drina bridge into Visegrad town aside from the one that you've testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was one and the same column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the entire column escorted to the football stadium in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the column of people, were there other people in the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For the most part, it was people from the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe what happened in the football stadium.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the football stadium, people positioned themselves in different places. Most everybody was on one part of the stadium. In the other part of the stadium there were soldiers. At that moment, an officer came. He introduced himself to all present by way of a megaphone with words to this effect: "I am Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic and I am commander of this town. So I am commanding this army that's here. We have the White Eagles units within our ranks, and they are under my command too. And now you will be going to certain places," and he enumerated all of them, and they were all around town. He said they were safe because they were under army control, and he said, among other things, that no resistance should be put up to the army. In case a single bullet is fired from any house in any village, he will level the house. If one soldier would be wounded in a village, the entire village would be levelled --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to the ground, and that is how the meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people who were gathered in the stadium, were they also searched by soldiers present at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So before they left the stadium, that's also what he explained over this microphone, the commander did. He established, I think, four or five columns. There were two soldiers for each, and everybody was searched for weapons or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the ethic make-up of the people gathered into the stadium on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only Bosniaks, Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many people at its greatest amount of Bosniaks or Muslims were gathered into the stadium during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is estimated that there were between 4.000 and 5.000 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were all of those 4.000 or 5.000 people searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think so. I did not wait for the very end of the search, but generally speaking, everybody was supposed to be searched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were all of those people told where and where they could not go when they left the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander explained that very precisely, where people were allowed to go and where they were not allowed to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were a large number of these people prohibited from returning to their homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this, did there come a time when you were summoned to a meeting in the Hotel Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the lieutenant colonel spoke to the people there, he said to me, "You, you will report to me now down there now at the Visegrad Hotel."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to the Visegrad Hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. People started going to the places where they were allowed to go, and I stopped by the hotel to report as ordered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have to wait for some period in the hotel lobby? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When I got to the hotel, then I was told that I had to wait for a while by the reception desk before the commander would receive me, so I waited there for a while, right at that spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were waiting there, were you able to tell where in the hotel the lieutenant colonel was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew where he was, in which room, but I waited at the reception desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when two people who came to see the lieutenant colonel where he was in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who they were that came to see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was waiting by the reception desk, at one point in time Biljana Plavsic came by. It is well known that she was vice-president of Republika Srpska. And Branimir Savovic. He was president of the Serbian Democratic Party for the municipality of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they go in to see the lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They went to the room where I was supposed to be at a meeting with the lieutenant colonel. Soon after that, I was told that I could go and that I could come the following day because right then the lieutenant colonel could not receive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd ask that a video be assigned a number. This is the video that I've put an extensive note in the summary. The way I propose to deal with this is after the video is to put on the split screen the two identical images for the witness and the Chamber to see and be able to compare that image with Exhibit 506 which was shown to B-127, if that's acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look at a video on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I could ask the usher just to ensure that it is set up for the Sanction display. There will be no sound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will pause it in several spots just to give you an opportunity to explain what it is that we are viewing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If we could begin the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe -- have you seen this video before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one? I don't know. I can't remember having seen this particular one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the video now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this the area of Visegrad that we are looking at on this video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The flag that we can see in this -- this portion of the video, do you recognise that flag or can you comment on that flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the flag is not the flag of Yugoslavia, and it's not the flag of the Yugoslav People's Army either. This is the kind of flag that was carried by Serb paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would note for the Chamber the entire video is four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The entire video is four minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, while we're watching this video, did you yourself actually drive the cameraman who shot this particular video during portions of this video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please identify the portion that you are actually the person driving the car.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When we come to that point, I'll signal it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be helpful if the witness tells us what we're looking at now. Mr. Groome, if you could establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Pause it there, please. We paused it at 1 minute, 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please describe what we have seen now in the first two minutes of the video.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until now, for the most part it was the outskirts of town that was filmed. The image before this one was from the direction of Uzice, the town from the direction of the Uzice, and buildings can be seen, and we could also see how these soldiers were coming. So for the most part, it was the town and its outskirts that were filmed from the direction of Uzice, facing Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this video shot at the time the JNA entered Visegrad or on the day or days that the JNA entered Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's it. As the soldiers were coming. It was the arrival of the soldiers that was filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you could describe what we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the part towards Visegrad. Now we see the outskirts of town again viewed from a helicopter, recorded from a helicopter. This is one of the bridges in Visegrad, the so-called new bridge. And in the very background, the old Turkish bridge can be seen too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the upper right-hand corner of the image; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again a panorama of town from a helicopter. This car, we see this car. This is the car that I drove, the one we can see now. This is what I drove, the TV crew. And now we see the recording from the helicopter again. The old bridge and the panorama of town. This is the hydroelectric power plant in Visegrad. It's about two kilometres away from the old bridge. Again the panorama. This is already the centre of town. We can say that. Now we see those trucks, those military trucks that were escorting the civilians who had come to town, the ones that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without identifying the person, as it may identify you, do you know some of the people in this truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Exactly. I know some of these people here very well. These are all details from town, various facilities in town. Again we can see the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're just calling up the two images from 506 and from this image.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you now to look at the two images on your screen and ask you to confirm whether or not they're not the same. The image on the left is from Prosecution Exhibit 506; the image on the right is from this exhibit, this video. Are they not the same video footage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear enough. I can't really say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will rely on the Chamber's -- I will rely on the Chamber's assessment of the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not clear. It's not focused, the image.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me if I'm mistaken, I don't believe we've assigned a number to this new video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not using P numbers here, for the registry. For the Prosecution it's just the straight number, 527.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if you could remind me who was the Serb journalist that gave evidence about the column that passed the Drina --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: His name is Jovan Dulovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You drew my attention last time to the fact that at the beginning, when starting my cross-examination, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. should point out when I consider the witness to be lying. I thought that was superfluous because I said about the whole indictment that it was false, but following your suggestion, I would like to say at the very outset that this witness, who is blaming the ethnic cleansing and what he said about the role of the JNA is absolutely not true and I think it is pure fabrication. And now we'll come to the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me tell you something else. The reason that you have to put, when you maintain the witness has not told the truth, has two other bases. First, the witness should have the opportunity of dealing with your allegations. You make serious allegations like that, the witness should have the opportunity of answering. It's only fair that they should. Second, the Trial Chamber should know what issues are in dispute and what are not. Merely to say you challenge everything is no answer. If there are specific facts which you challenge, you should do so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my cross-examination, I will show it. I am not challenging the fact that Witness 1505 is from Visegrad. I'm not challenging the fact that he lived there. Certainly not. But I am challenging the fact that allegedly the army engaged in ethnic cleansing, and we will see even from this video footage that these are things that have nothing to do with his testimony. But anyway, I think you saw that for yourself. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1505, is it true that you personally - not anyone other than you but you yourself - regarding the sabotage group which was -- consisted of Niha Dizdarevic, Faho Isic [phoen], Mufa Muftasic [phoen], and Fikret Sacirevic who prepared explosive devices, that you provided explosives for their activities in view of the position you held --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let the witness deal with this. First of all, the accused is suggesting there was a sabotage group, and he's mentioned three names. And secondly, he is suggesting that you provided explosives for them. Those are the two questions, and you should have the opportunity to answer them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let him deal with it, Mr. Milosevic. You make these allegations, he must have the opportunity to deal with it in a fairly orderly way. Yes. First of all, do you agree that there was a sabotage group or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I'm not aware of the existence of such a sabotage group. Judging by the names, I know of one, I never heard of two others, as regards the first part of the question. As for the second part of the question, that I procured explosives for them, that also is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness said, like you did, that I mentioned three names. I actually mentioned five names, and you will probably be able to check that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, they didn't hear all five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on to some other specifics, do you recall that on the 19th of September, 1991, an act of sabotage was carried out at the railway tunnel at Dobrun while simultaneously explosives were planted under the viaduct on the Belgrade-Bar railroad. This was on the 19th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not heard of those events.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're getting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session if you want to ask any more of these questions. Private session. We'll go into private session and see how we get on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. 1505, is it true that after the multi-party elections in Visegrad in 1990 pressures started and threats and physical assaults on the Serbs, and even slogans to the effect that the Serbs should be exterminated from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since it is absolutely not true, do you recall that the Muslim extremists, the brother of the vice-president of the Party of Democratic Action in Visegrad, the monument to Ivo Andric was destroyed on the 1st of July, 1991, on liberation square in Visegrad? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that fact, of that event, but this was not directed again the Serbs directly. It was an isolated event. And Ivo Andric anyway wasn't a Serb. He was a Croat. If you mean that this was meant as a threat to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serbs consider him to be a Serb. If you consider him to be a Croat, that's up to you. But what do you think was the motive for destroying that monument, and that on the 1st of July, 1991? It was broken with a hammer that was used in quarries normally. It was thrown into the Drina, destroyed by a sledgehammer in fact. Isn't that right, Mr. 1505?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When speaking about that event, this was not organised in any way by the authorities or anyone else. It was purely one of those incidents. Afterwards, criminal proceedings were instituted against the person who did this. So this was nothing so special. You would see nowadays at a football match people would break a chair or something else and then they would be punished for it and that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So breaking chairs at a football match and destroying a monument in the centre of town to the only Nobel Prize winner from these areas of the former Yugoslavia to you is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was an incident carried out by one or two citizens. What they wanted to achieve, because this was a monument to a well-known figure, they wanted to attract attention to themselves, and that for doing this they were punished because of this incident. This was an incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that they were punished for this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for certain that proceedings were instituted and conducted. Now, how the whole thing ended, I can't be a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know for sure that proceedings were conducted. An investigation was carried out, and those men went to court. Now, how the whole thing ended --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume you know that too, or are you claiming you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I don't know what the punishment was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone published for this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If there is a case in court, then they will find out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But that is a generalised view. But you don't really know whether they were really punished or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure they were, but I don't know whether it was a fine or some sort of a prison term or how high the fine was. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was an administrative complication or confusion. It was a pecuniary fine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no confusion, a normal court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you remember a leaflet in August 1991 distributed throughout Visegrad with 20 instructions as to what should be done to the Serbs to expel them or destroy them? Among other things, there was a message: "Do not allow your children to play with them. Empty your garbage in front of their doors. Urinate in their entrances. Mark their houses and apartments. Write graffiti with threats on their homes and churches." 20 different instructions on a leaflet that was distributed in August 1991. I assume that this is something that you could not have missed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise for this, but I have to say that this is a lie and not what the gentleman said a moment ago. I never heard of this in my whole life, and that had something like this happened, I should have known about it. I must have known about it. This was all made up. Everything that the gentleman has said has been fabricated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the event of the 13th of April, 1992, when Murat Sabanovic, who also destroyed the monument to Ivo Andric, threatened to destroy the hydro power plant in Visegrad, and when Alija Izetbegovic sent him a message over the radio waves, "Don't, Murat, yet. It's not time yet." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this was on the radio, so I just happened to hear it on the radio, as did half of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As to whether Alija Izetbegovic responded with such a message, I hear it for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And when the time did come several days later, he opened one of the gates at the dam and the water inflicted considerable material damage and human casualties downstream along the Drina, precisely in the area inhabited by Serbs; is that right? Or maybe you don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that very well, and I will respond, Your Honours. There was material damage but not to such a large extent as one might think. The water did cause damages but exclusively in this case the material damage was inflicted on Bosniaks, on Muslims, because their houses were close to the river. Not a single Serb suffered any material damage as a result of this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that the water that flooded an area, fortunately the dam was not blown up though he threatened to blow it up. You know that, don't you? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same Murat Sabanovic who broke up the monument to Ivo Andric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the man who broke the monument is threatening to blow up the dam, and then he doesn't do that, but he opens a gate and the water floods an area downstream. And you claim that the water selectively caused damage to the Muslims and not the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I clarify this? I am not claiming that the water was selective in any sense, but it so happened that the houses along the banks were Bosniak houses. This is a pure coincidence on the one hand. And on the other, the lake which was north of Visegrad is of a larger capacity than the lake above Visegrad. And the hydro power station in Bajina Basta was emptied so there was absolutely no danger because the lower lake, as we -- if we can call it that, was of greater capacity than the one above. As for destroying the dam, one might say that this is almost ridiculous, that someone who hasn't got anything to destroyed a 40-metre high dam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to you, this was no serious threat. It was more like a joke, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, sir, it was not a joke, but such a serious event. He wasn't alone. There was this man, Murat Sabanovic, that you mentioned. He lived close to the power station, maybe 500 metres away, and both he and his neighbours went to the power station out of fear, and in a feeling of agony they threatened, "If you capture us, we will blow up the hydro power station." And it was quite clear to everyone that he couldn't even destroy a bit of the power plant, never mind blow it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, for instance, that in an interview, as you said a moment ago that this person who destroyed the monument was not fully responsible, that an interview on the 18th of February, 2000, to the Sarajevo Oslobodjenje, Murat Sabanovic declared that the destruction of the monument was ordered by Ejub Ganic and Omer Mehmet [phoen]. Do you know that that is what he stated in the Sarajevo newspaper Oslobodjenje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that that same Murat Sabanovic, with his extremist group which included Ibrahim Demir, Zulja Subasic, Nusret Velagic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Make sure there is no mistake about these names which you reel off and then it's very difficult for the interpreters and indeed everybody else. Now, we'll get the names and we'll ask the witness about them. Was Murat Sabanovic in an extremist group? Perhaps the witness would answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There was no extremist group, so this man couldn't have been a member of a group that didn't exist. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know Demir Ibrahim, Zijad Subasic, and Nusret Velagic? Are you familiar about those names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of these three gentlemen that you mentioned, I know Nusret Velagic as he was a waiter and that is how I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that Sabanovic, together with this group, which included these persons that I have just slowly and carefully read out, as early as 1990 would stop vehicles passing by from Serbia and harass the passengers, ordinary tourists? And even buses carrying children and elderly people who were travelling to visit some places of interest? Are you aware of those incidents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear. I did not say that this group existed, and I claim that it did not exist. As for certain incidents, they probably did occur before and after and always this happens among citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since you say that all of this happened before, later and that there are always some kind of incidents among citizens, are you aware of the arrest of Nermin Sisic, a criminal on the 14th of June, 1991, which was used in order to cause clashes with the police and unrest in general? May I jog your memory? This Murat and Alija Sabanovic broke into the building of the Secretariat of the Interior in an attempt to seize weapons, and they put forth a request that members of the police force who were ethnic Serbs should be dismissed immediately. I'm even giving you the date, the 14th of June, 1991. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that by chance, about this incident, as you called it, although you said quite a few things that are false in this context. I happen to know this young man who lived in my neighbourhood, and I know that once he committed some kind of a violation, so of course he was taken by the police. And as for all the rest, you just added it up of your own free will. It's an insinuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have information about that, Mr. 1505. I was not in Visegrad myself at that time, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not inform you well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the night between the 2nd and 3rd of August, 1991, the municipal -- from the Municipal Secretariat of National Defence all documents of military conscripts were stolen, and Miralem Ibisevic, and Mesic Tvrtkovic took part in that? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this particular case from you right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in September 1991, when for no reason whatsoever Milija Cebic, a Serb, was beaten up? He was then transferred to hospital in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know about this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you say that there was an incident then. I don't know about that. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that this same Murat Sabanovic on the 8th of October, 1991, organised an armed attack on the police station in Visegrad because they had arrested his brother Avdija, although this brother of his was released on the very same day in the late afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had something like that happened, I would have had to know about it. It's ridiculous, Your Honours. I must say that what is being presented here is practically ridiculous, that one man would attack a police station that had about 240 policemen there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is it funny or ridiculous that Ranko Baranac, a Serb, was killed in his village also towards the end of 1991, and Hasan Sabanija shot him in the chest? He was a security worker in a Visegrad company. This man was killed. Are you aware of that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I happen to know about this incident because this Hasan is a neighbour. He was a neighbour. And of course people know what happens to their neighbours. It was not an interethnic conflict. They had a purely personal relationship. Not to go into all of it here and now, it had to do with women, and they fought ultimately. And this man you mentioned, Hasan, was in prison because he committed this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, this Hasan Sabanija killed Ranko Baranac; is that right? This was towards the end of 1991. You know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I do apologise, Your Honours. But there was a fight. They fought. They were both at each others, and this Hasan who survived was sent to prison. I know that for sure because he's a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you know about the murder, but you just treat it as some kind of a little squabble of theirs; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was simply a conflict between two men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that on the 24th of March, 1992 the workers of SUP Visegrad left work because on the day before that armed Muslim groups took over town, took over the police station too and started looting property, taking away the property of Serbs, their cars, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an inversion. The Serb policemen had left the official institution where the police had been. I don't know whether it was exactly on that date, but for a while it was the case but not for the reasons the gentleman has just mentioned. It was explicitly ordered to them by the Serb Democratic Party. That's why they did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. 1505, this threat to destroy the dam in Visegrad, which was not only a threat, water did flow but the dam was not blown up, this happened on the 13th of April, 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could have been that date, somewhere around that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So everything I'm saying happened before that. And then part of the units of the Uzice Corps, on the 15th of April according to what you said, came to Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are several questions there. It was not caused by one another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it caused by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've confused me a bit now. I mean you have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's start again. Ask your questions in an orderly way so the witness can follow them and answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, the dam was taken and the threat was made to blow it up. In response to this provocation which was a serious threat with unforeseen consequences, two days later, a unit of the Uzice Corps came to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Stop there. Stop there and allow the witness to answer the questions. What is suggested is that the Uzice Corps or part of it came to Visegrad on the 15th of April, two days after the threat. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The second part of the question is this, if you can answer it, you may not be able to: Did it arrive as a result of the threat to the dam? Was that the reason or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can give an answer to that too. This was not the cause. This was not the reason why the Uzice Corps came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since only a minute ago, as you mentioned Captain Vuksavljevic, you sitting in this room here said that Captain Vuksavljevic was commander of the unit that was protecting the dam; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other day when you started your testimony, you said that Captain Vukosavljevic came to Visegrad and that's when the Uzice Corps came, the 15th of April, that is. You said that yourself. And you said just now that he commanded the force protecting the dam. Isn't it clear why they came to Visegrad? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is correct that Captain Vuksavljevic was commander of the dam. However, this was just a small part of the Uzice Corps, a very small unit as compared to the number of soldiers in the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it being disputed that the danger of destroying the dam could have caused a catastrophe in the lower part of the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I explained that a few minutes ago but I can repeat that. If the dam were to break, either by way of a natural disaster or if it were to be destroyed artificially since the lower lake had been emptied, it certainly could not have jeopardised anything in the lower part of the Drina. I think that that is a sufficient answer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you claim that the destruction of the dam in Visegrad would not have caused any kind of major problems. Is that your assertion, Mr. 1505?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that question several times, so there's no need for him to do it again. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We got the order right, so let's just go back to one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the work you did and in view of the activities you had, you are aware of the broader political context. Is it correct that tensions grew after the referendum on the independence of Bosnia that was held without the Serbs? Is it correct that on the following day conflicts started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum is a well-known thing. As for that in particular - how should I put this? - changing things, I don't know. Well, perhaps the question is not specific enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that immediately after the referendum the killings of Serbs started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day after the referendum in Sarajevo people were killed as they attended a wedding, a Serb wedding, and they were killed by the Green Berets, and it is known who killed them too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with the witness. You can ask people, and you have done, who can give evidence about Sarajevo, about these allegations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you know that in Visegrad the population of Serb ethnicity did not take part in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The referendum was organised at the level of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it was not a municipal referendum. It was, rather, a referendum of the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some people voted in the referendum, others did not, like any other country in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, like in any other country in the world. Some voted and some did not. It just so happened that the Serbs did not vote.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you really think that I'm responsible for the results of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are co-responsible because you held a high position, and you certainly took part in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we're not getting anywhere with this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember further on the rise in tensions, the fighting in Sarajevo after that, the attacks at the military convoy in Tuzla and so on, a series of events that caused a great deal of unrest and considerable casualties among the Serbs at that time. Perhaps I can put it that way. Do you remember that, Mr. 1505?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, as for these events, like everybody else, I could see some of it on television, so I mostly know from television what was going on. But it's not true that these were events where Serbs were the victims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. There is information about that. And do you know, since you were in a position then to know, that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, though incomplete, on the 4th of April, 1992, passed a decision to mobilise units of the Territorial Defence, the police, and the civilian protection in spite of all warnings that a peaceful settlement could be found only by way of an agreement among all three peoples? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were such orders. I don't know exactly what the date was. It could hardly be the 4th of April, though. It was after the attacks that started against the city itself, and that's when the Presidency passed this decision, as far as I can remember. But of course this is outside the scope of my powers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But General Nambiar says that there were no attacks on the town or shelling until the 3rd of May when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't possibly answer what General Nambiar says. It has nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 12th of April, 1992, Izetbegovic issued directives to the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence for an all-out attack on JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear of such an order for the first time here and now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, since this is within this context, the context we're discussing, you, in your statement - let me briefly refer to this - you say that the vice-president of the Serbian Democratic Party was Stanko Pecikoza. "I heard that he was killed by the SDS, that is, by his own party because he helped the Muslims to leave town. He helped me and my family to get out of Visegrad. He took a lot of families out. He could do that because he was the vice-president of the party. Not long after I was taken out by him, I heard that he was killed." Is it possible that you are claim that the vice-president of the Serbian Democratic Party was killed by his own party members because he helped Muslims to leave town and he helped you and your family? And you know that he was killed by the Serbian Democratic Party for the motives that you have indicated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing in particular to add or subtract from what I said earlier on, and I said that I heard that that is how it was. Of course I wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You heard about it. But doesn't what you claim here in connection with the killing of the vice-president of the Serbian Democratic Party and something else also, doesn't that mean that the Muslims were voluntarily leaving the town with someone's assistance rather than being expelled from town? Isn't that so, Mr. 1505?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was very difficult to leave town, and you needed someone who was influential or prestigious to take you out of town. No one was leaving voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know what you mean because I can read as well. Well doesn't that mean that no one was expelling the Muslims from town, that it was difficult to leave for the -- because of the security situation is one thing, but doesn't this mean that no one was expelling the Muslims, wasn't chasing them out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what it was was that people paid a lot of money to leave because their life wasn't worth a pfennig in town, a cent. They were absolutely unprotected by the authorities. They were ignored by the authorities. Anyone could kill a Bosniak in those days without being called to account. And that is why it was difficult to leave town. That is what I meant. It was difficult to find a connection whereby you would leave town and save your life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1505. The point of my question was that no one was chasing the Muslims out of town. Is that clear at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first part, yes, but later on it was closed and one couldn't leave voluntarily. Even those who wanted to couldn't. Actually, everybody wanted to leave because they were not at all safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the events around the dam, we established that on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 13th they threatened to blow it up. On the 15th, units of the Uzice Corps arrived. You mentioned shooting on the 4th of April, 1992 at Seval Delibasic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that there was no investigation. Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation boiled down to stating the facts and taking note of them in the MUP or SUP offices and they didn't make an on-site inspection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And you say that on the 5th of April, 1992 there was more shooting in the village of Dobrun. Didn't it right that you don't know who was shooting or at whom they were shooting, that there was shooting in Dobrun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for who was doing the shooting, one cannot assert with certainty, but who was being shot at, that is known. That is the fire was opened at the settlement and the people living in it, and they were exclusively Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraphs 14 and 16 of you statement, you say that fighting started everywhere around Visegrad. Mortar fire was directed against various parts of Visegrad. We will come back to that context, but tell me now, is it true that the people who were regulating positions were wearing uniforms and civilian clothes and that that had nothing to do with the JNA, what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were regulating military positions in the environs of the town, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that has nothing to do with the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it has some direct and indirect connection to the JNA, because according to what I know, the JNA supervised and controlled this to a high degree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could it have done that when you say that they arrived on the 15th of April, 1992? How could it have supervised and controlled anything before that? You saw them for the first time on the 15th of April, 1992, after the threat was made to blow up the dam.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you are making an inversion of things. Units of the Uzice Corps that were combat units, in large numbers and well equipped, they arrived around the 15th. But before that, they need not have been a unit to supervise and control and give instructions. These were small numbers of people, two, three, five, ten men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, these two, three, five or ten men, they were not JNA, were they, Mr. 1505?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, if we hadn't noticed their vehicles and a helicopter which only the army had, it would be difficult to say. But as they were seen, then it can be said with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the video, we see a small helicopter, a Gazelle that only does reconnoitering or transport an officer or a wounded man from one position to another. It is not at all a combat aircraft. You showed it here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this case on the video footage it is a helicopter, but you must admit the army has a large number of helicopters of different types, and this is not the same one that I'm referring to. When I say that helicopters were seen, I'm not referring to this video footage in this particular case, but I'm referring to an earlier period, earlier on, maybe a month or two before the event that the gentleman is asking about, the event linked to the dam. Military vehicles were seen and military helicopters that were landing at the place where military positions were being regulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Did you see a single military helicopter active anywhere, actually being active?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any period, right up until the army arrived on the 15th of April, did a military helicopter operate in any sense? What are you saying? What are you telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 15th of April there were no actions by military helicopters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any actions from any military vehicle or by any unit, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no such actions that were visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. There were no actions that were visible. Okay. Talking about helicopters, let us finish with this video footage. The helicopter is taking a cameraman filming the surroundings of Visegrad. I didn't see anything more than that. And on one part of the footage one can see quite clearly soldiers going along the road in a column, JNA soldiers with helmets, going in formation order, regularly dressed, and their distinguishing feature are the helmets on their heads. And then quite separately, in a separate clip, you see men wearing -- carrying a different flag and moving along some other road. That is all that could be seen on your video recording; is that right, Mr. 1505? What else did you show us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't show anything in particular apart from what was on the footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what can be seen on this video footage that you consider to be important? There is this group of soldiers that probably belong to the Uzice Corps, if that's what you say, that they were there, that were moving in formation order, wearing helmets and moving along the road, securing the area. And then after that, you have some men carrying a flag, and it is quite clear that they're not JNA - you can see by their caps, by their clothing - carrying a flag along the road. Again there are no actions, and so what if we're carrying a flag? What is all this about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to answer the significance of the evidence. It's for the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's not for the witness to answer the significance of the evidence. It's for the Prosecution and, ultimately, for the Trial Chamber. We've seen it. You can make any comments about it you like, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1505, you showed, from a car that you say you were driving, some shots of certain parts of Visegrad. And what is seen on those shots?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask the witness what he saw, but I've told you that the significance of what is on the video is a matter entirely for us. Now, what you can tell us, Mr. B-1505, is what you saw when you were driving the car, if you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, it's not really a very concrete question. With me was a crew from TV Belgrade with a camera and this is a very exhaustive, long question. Could he be more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you can't answer, let's not waste time. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the TV Belgrade crew ask you, as an inhabitant of Visegrad, without specifying any further, that you drive them around Visegrad to show them what things were like? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did ask someone to show them the way, where they were going. And at the end, I was implicitly ordered to do it. However, everything ended up well, luckily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean luckily or not? You take a crew of cameramen into your car and drive them around town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under normal circumstances, that would be perfectly normal. But after all, these were extraordinary circumstances. There were no inhabitants in town, there were soldiers, paramilitaries roaming around, so it was rather risky. But anyway, it all went well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, you say in paragraph 18 that you spoke to a certain Savovic about ending the shooting because people were getting killed and the SDS wanted the police to split. That is what you say in point 18. Would you be kind enough to explain this for me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, the statement has a broader context, and to explain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it I would have to cover a broader context. It is true that what you read out is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what I'm asking you to explain, please. You spoke to a certain Savovic for the shooting to stop, and the SDS wanted the police to split. That is what you say. What was the cause of this? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it wasn't just anyone. Savovic was president of the Serbian Democratic Party for Visegrad and commander of the Serbian War Presidency, and under his command there were various attacks from various directions on the town. And it is for those reasons that we negotiated with them the -- that they stop the shelling. And they asked that the police be divided up, that they have separate offices of their own, et cetera, and these various facilities, but that was not a cause and effect. These were different things. He was earlier on in the Serbian Democratic Party when they made these requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a moment, please. Now, look at your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it. It's not marked. Paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the 18th paragraph in order. It is on page 4, the last paragraph. I will read it out to you: "I talked to Savovic about stopping the shooting because people were dying. The SDS had asked for the division of the police." And I draw your attention to the next sentence without leaving anything out: "They had asked for this about ten days before the shooting started." So they asked for the division of the police ten days before the shooting started; is that right? And I quote: "Also, about 12 Serbs in uniform had been captured by the regular police force in Babin Potok; this was once the shooting started in Visegrad. Some of these captured Serbs were wearing the regular police uniforms and some had camouflage uniforms. I know this because later I released them and saw them." Will you please explain this. You mentioned the other day when you were testifying that these 12 Serb policemen were released after the JNA had arrived. They were liberated after the JNA arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I need to answer that question? If it's a question, yes, I can answer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you had finished your question. So the sequence of events is correct. These people were released. The date of their release was after the JNA arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're telling us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we move on, it's time now for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes and resume cross-examination then when you will have 20 minutes more, Mr. Milosevic. Yes. Yes, you've had well over -- you've had over an hour already. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a 92 bis witness, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It is a transcript witness. Yes. We will adjourn, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear anything. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Get your microphone on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this witness said himself a short while ago that as far as events that I'm asking him about, he would have had to know about them because he was there, and I have a considerable number of questions for him, and that's why I'm asking you for more time so that I could put these questions to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider -- at the moment, 20 minutes. We will consider how you take your time and whether it's being properly spent, but just go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the JNA came, it liberated these 12 captive Serb policemen. Is that right, Witness 1505?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way it was. It wasn't the JNA who freed them. The legal authorities were still in place, and they reached a decision to release these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why were these 12 Serb policemen taken captive? Was that also done by these legal authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These 12 Serb policemen were taken prisoner because they were outside the regular units of the police, or outside the regular units of the Territorial Defence, and they were, therefore, taken prisoner by the units of the Territorial Defence legally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So they were taken prisoner by the units of the Territorial Defence. You're trying to say Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not only Muslim units. In these units there was a still -- there was still a mixed composition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 27 that there were no weapons on the Muslim side which could be used by someone to open fire. So how did these unarmed units then take these people prisoner in the first place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police and the Territorial Defence had a certain number of infantry weapons. That is what they were equipped with regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct, then, that the army issued an order that all weapons should be taken away and that then, when the army came, the action of disarming paramilitary formations started? Is that right or is that not right, Mr. 1505?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that the army was disarming some paramilitary formations. The only paramilitary formations were, in fact, on the side of the army. The army disarmed regular units. They took away the weapons that people had had in peacetime, that is to say, hunting weapons, personal weapons, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before that, you said yourself that there had been shooting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that there had been shooting from the surrounding hills, mostly aimed at town or the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you described that second meeting of yours, the one that you came to, you say that officers who talked there in front of you were saying that the right bank of the Drina was clear, that the left bank should be inspected, that it should be seen what was there. So was that an activity that was aimed at taking weapons away and alleviating the situation in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, by your leave, I'm going to give a broader answer. This is a meeting with Colonel Ojdanic at the military barracks. I was supposed to come to this meeting from a different part of town, and then indeed considerable gunfire could be heard from the other side. I telephoned to the dam to -- I phoned Lieutenant Colonel Vukosavljevic but there is such heavy gunfire on the right side that I don't dare come. And he said, "All right. It's going to stop now." And soon after that the shooting started [as interpreted] and I went there. Not much is required on that score to conclude what is to be concluded about the people who were shooting from the right bank to the left bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, why do you link up the word "clear" with some kind of ethnic cleansing? "Clear" here means safe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this word "clear" was used, then there is no doubt that this meant there was no Bosniak Muslim population left there. It can also be interpreted in this other way, that it was safe, but knowing that all the people from that area had withdrawn before the Yugoslav People's Army and crossed over to other places, then the word "clear" means that there was no more Bosniak Muslim population there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't that mean that there are no armed formations left there? It doesn't refer to the population. Are you trying to say that the JNA was conducting ethnic cleansing in the area of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you can mean by that is up to you, but I know and I claim that where the army came, people would leave the area. Nobody would stay behind. If somebody would stay behind - I know a few such cases of people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who stayed behind - they lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I'm asking you about this particular event now. You said yourself that Ojdanic had promised to protect to the entire civilian population. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next day, when talking to Captain Vukosavljevic, whom you mention, Vukosavljevic with his unit went to that village which is 5 or 6 kilometres from the centre of town in order to escort them to town because they were in peril there because of the armed operations. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put quite a few things right, although these people were not in peril because of armed operations, because nobody had opposed the arrival of the JNA, so nobody shot at them. On the other hand, Your Honours, if we look at the map a bit more precisely, then you will see the place where these people were grouped, they were not grouped in a voluntary basis -- on a voluntary basis. They were simply corralled there, if I can put it that way. The only road from there led to town. On the other side was the Drina or mountains, impenetrable mountains. So the only road from there was to town. It's not -- it was no accident that they were there, that they were corralled there. This was done on the basis of a plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1505, on the basis of what you've been saying, it was my understanding that you personally went with Captain Vukosavljevic in order to make sure that these people are safely transferred to town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I went with Captain Vukosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that was your request for the army to help so that these people would safely arrive in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the army went to protect these people, the assumption is that the army was not shooting at these people, the army did not go there to protect them from the army itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, again by your leave, a bit of an extensive answer. It is true that we requested the army to protect people because I explained a short while ago the situation that they were in. It was a situation with no way out. They could not go there, anywhere. There was no road leaving -- leading anywhere. People were panic-stricken because they realised that on the north was the Drina. On the other side was the impenetrable mountain. Their only possible salvation could have been if the army were to take them to town somehow and put them under their protection, if I can put it that way, because there was no other choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did the army protect these people? Precisely what you asked for, that the army should go and make sure that these people could safely get to town and be under their protection. Didn't the army protect them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment, the army did protect them, and they did their job properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were not carrying out ethnic cleansing. They were protecting civilians. Tell me now, please, in paragraph 28 you say that you from the TO were in contact with the authorities in Sarajevo and that you received instructions only from Sarajevo about what was going on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the Territorial Defence. That is a bit of a mistake. Instructions did come from Sarajevo. So it was the decisions of the Presidency that were being carried out and of the legal government that then existed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you say that they were carrying out instructions of the government from Sarajevo. Is it correct then that a decision was passed concerning the blockade of JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear of such an order. It never came to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that it was precisely the effect of these decisions that the military equipment of the JNA could not be withdrawn from various garrisons in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I did not see such a decision. I was not in that kind of position so as to receive such instructions or things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear at all about various attacks against the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I know about that is primarily from the media. Everybody could have heard that, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything about significant arms deliveries carried out for the Muslim forces as far as back as October 1991, almost six months prior to the outbreak of the armed conflict, a large quantity of automatic rifles and other weapons? There is even a study of Jacques Merlinot published in Paris in 1993. This is a French author.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not in a position to know such things. What I know out of all of this is that there weren't any special Muslim units. I know about legal units, the police, the Territorial Defence. This was under the command and the authority of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Since this was under the command of the Presidency, do you remember that it was precisely this Presidency that at the beginning of April passed a decree to abolish the republican TO headquarters and organise a TO staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this same decree relieved of duty Lieutenant Colonel Drago Vukosavljevic who was commander until then and appointed Hasanefendic commander from thereon? All of this was the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I was not in such a position. How should I put this? I could not have known about things like that. I had personal obligations of my own, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it being disputed that from the beginning of April when Hasanefendic -- well, as a matter of fact, he even says in his own book that from the first days when the statehood was renewed, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina establishes its own unit. So after 1878 and 1941, it is the first time that Bosnia has its own army again. This was already on the 8th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, this is where we waste time and you take up your 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's not waste any time. I think I have not spent this time in vain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about weapon deliveries to the Muslim side when a Boeing 747 flew in from Iran via Slovenia and to Croatia? Lord Owen writes about this in his Balkan Odyssey. This was in the summer of 1992 when this delivery took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, obviously you have more time than I do. You read more books than I have. I really haven't read this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know anything about these weapons? I'm not asking you about whether you read any books. I'm asking you about whether you know about the arms supplies and all of this that happened after the events that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1505 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, see, at the very outset you said that my entire statement is false, so I don't see why you would believe me if I told you something about that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm telling you that what you're saying about ethnic commencing is false, and about your meeting too, because practically what you said later refuted the former, because the army had protected you. It did not ethnically cleanse anybody. So do you know that the fifth round of the BH conference took place on the 17th of March in Sarajevo and that Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and Boban, leaders of the nationalist parties had signed a declaration about the constitutional order of Bosnia-Herzegovina? This is known as the Cutileiro plan named after Cutileiro, a Portuguese diplomat.
